categories.name: Scores & ratings
categories.blurb: How data become scores, ranks and tiers.

terms.definition: The headline risk score, from 0 to 100: a weighted average of the four pillar scores. 0 = the lowest risk in the sample, 100 = the highest.
Any indicator or pillar put on a common 0–100 scale, where 100 = the riskiest country in the sample that year.
Scores compare countries with each other in the same year. They are not probabilities, and a low score means 'safer than most countries', which can still be dangerous.
How most indicators become risk scores: a country's position among all countries, from safest (0) to riskiest (100).
Used for battle deaths and displacement, which are zero for most countries: 'none' scores 0 and the score rises steeply from the first deaths or displacements, then flattens.
A country's position among all scored countries; 1 = the highest risk. Ranks within a region or peer group count the same way.
Five bands of the composite score: Low (under 20), Moderate (20 to under 40), Elevated (40 to under 60), High (60 to under 80) and Severe (80 to 100).
One of four groups of indicators: Political Stability & Violence, Governance & Institutions, Macroeconomic & Financial, and Social & Humanitarian Pressure.
A single measured data series, such as inflation or rule of law. The index uses 17.
How much each pillar counts in the composite. Defaults: Stability 35%, Governance 25%, Economy 25%, Social 15%; you can change them in the sidebar.
The share of the 17 indicators available for a country. Below 75%, treat its score with extra caution.
The middle score among countries in the same region, used as a benchmark.
The countries a profile is compared with: the same region, the same income group, or all.
The composite now minus last year's: ▲ riskier by a point or more, ▼ safer by a point or more, ■ less than a point either way.
The index recomputed for every year since 2015, each time with only the data available for that year.
The pillar that moved most in the same direction as the composite since last year.
Recomputes a country's score with equal weights, or with one pillar left out, to show how much the result depends on modelling choices.
Change a country's indicators, or pick a scenario such as a currency crisis, and see how its score, tier and rank would move.
A test of the index: of the countries at peace in a year, did those where armed conflict broke out the next year already score high? Shown on the Methodology page.
The chance that a country where conflict broke out had scored higher than one where it did not: 0.5 is a coin flip, 1 is perfect.
A comparison with an independent index measuring something similar, here the Fragile States Index, to see where the two agree and where they differ.
Flagged, Partly flagged or Missed: what the index said the year before a major event, decided by a fixed rule (tier, rank and change over three years).

link.label: Wikipedia articles on the case-study events

terms.definition: A one-page summary of a country (score, pillars, trend, red flags and what it means in real life) to download from its profile.
Countries scoring 50+ that got 2+ points riskier, crossed a new red flag, or face a high-significance event within 120 days.

The estimated chance that armed conflict (25+ battle deaths) starts next year in a country at peace, from a small statistical model on the pillars, low-level violence and recent conflict. On the Conflict page and each country's Summary.
Testing a model on years it has not seen: each year is predicted by a model fitted only on earlier years, then compared with what happened.
How much better the predicted chances are than always guessing the average rate: 0 = no better, above 0 = better.
Whether predicted chances match what happened: of the cases given about 10%, about one in ten should see conflict.
A country's predicted chance divided by the average chance for countries at peace.

Apply one economic shock (say, growth −4 points) to many countries at once and see who crosses a tier or a red flag. Countries hit are scored against today's values, so a shock that hits everyone still shows.
The countries whose four pillar scores are closest to a country's, wherever they are in the world.
Mark countries to keep them on the Global overview and in Find. The list stays in your browser; no account needed.
The address of the Compare and Stress test pages holds your selection, so you can send it.
Every table behind the index, free to download as CSV, Excel or JSON on the Data downloads page, with a data dictionary.

categories.name: The 17 indicators
categories.blurb: Every data series in the score, by pillar.

terms.definition: Perceptions of the likelihood of political instability and politically motivated violence, including terrorism. Higher score = more stable.
Deaths in state-based armed conflicts (UCDP definition), scaled by population. Countries with no recorded conflict are scored 0.
A proxy for criminal violence and the state's control over security.
Citizens' ability to choose their government; freedom of expression, association and media.
Quality of public services and the civil service, and the credibility of policy commitments.
Ability to formulate and implement sound policies that permit private-sector development.
Confidence in contract enforcement, property rights, the police and the courts.
The extent to which public power is exercised for private gain, including state capture.
Current-year IMF estimate. High inflation erodes incomes and is a classic trigger of unrest.
Current-year IMF estimate. Recessions strain budgets, jobs and political support.
Current-year IMF estimate. High debt limits room to respond to shocks.
Current-year IMF estimate. Large deficits signal pressure for austerity or money printing.
Current-year IMF estimate. Persistent deficits create dependence on foreign financing.

terms.term: Total reserves in months of imports
terms.definition: The buffer against a currency or balance-of-payments crisis. Under 3 months is a common warning line.
Share of the labour force without work (IMF estimate used where the ILO series is missing).
tags: ILO modelled estimate via World Bank WDI

terms.definition: A well-documented driver of protest movements.
tags: ILO modelled estimate via World Bank WDI

terms.term: Forcibly displaced people from the country
terms.definition: Refugees, asylum seekers, others in need of international protection and internally displaced people originating from the country, as a share of its population.

categories.name: Warnings
categories.blurb: Absolute red lines that apply wherever a country ranks.

terms.definition: An absolute warning threshold, such as inflation of 20% or more. Unlike the relative score, it applies wherever the country ranks.
A red-flag threshold the country crosses today. '⚑ New' means it was crossed since last year.
Red-flag severities, from most to least severe: Critical (e.g. war, inflation ≥ 50%), Serious (e.g. active conflict, inflation ≥ 20%), Watch (e.g. debt ≥ 90% of GDP).
An indicator within reach of a threshold, for example inflation between 15% and 20%. Shown on each country's Summary.
A Watch flag raised when the WGI political-stability score falls by 5+ points over 3 years.

categories.name: Analyst assessments
categories.blurb: Terms from risk and intelligence writing.

terms.definition: The model tier comes from the data; the analyst rating is a human judgment that can differ, with the reason written down.
The expected direction over the horizon: Improving, Stable or Deteriorating.
How solid the evidence behind an assessment is: Low, Moderate or High.
The period an assessment looks ahead: 6, 12 or 24 months.
Bottom line up front: the two or three sentences a busy reader needs first.
A specific, checkable statement about the future, with a probability attached.
Standard words for probabilities from the US Intelligence Community, so words and numbers agree: 'unlikely' = 20–45%, 'likely' = 55–80%, 'very likely' = 80–95%, and so on.
A coherent story of how events could unfold: a base case, an upside and a downside, with probabilities adding to 100%.
An observable event that would show a scenario is coming true.
A political, security, economic or social force that pushes risk up or down.

categories.name: Conflict & displacement
categories.blurb: Armed conflict, violence and people forced from their homes.

terms.definition: Deaths in fighting between organised armed groups where at least one side is a government (UCDP 'state-based conflict'), counted where they happen.
25 or more battle-related deaths in a year (the UCDP threshold).
1,000 or more battle-related deaths in a year (the UCDP threshold).
People forced from their homes by conflict, violence or persecution: refugees, asylum seekers, others in need of international protection and internally displaced people.
A person who has fled across an international border and is recognised as needing protection.
A person who has applied for protection in another country and is waiting for a decision.
Someone forced from home who is still inside their own country.

terms.term: Others in need of international protection
terms.definition: People outside their country who need protection but have not applied for asylum (a UNHCR category since 2022).
The number of people from one origin country living in one host country.
A country where refugees and asylum seekers from elsewhere live.
Intentional killings per 100,000 people a year, a measure of criminal violence.
The share of world news coverage that mentions a country together with protests, riots, strikes or unrest (GDELT): a fast signal of unrest getting attention.
A country with at least 5 UCDP events or 25 deaths in the last 90 days, an Escalating signal, or a composite score of 60 or more.

The conflict-news signal on Hotspots: the share of news about a country that mentions fighting in the last 7 days against its usual level over 90 days. Escalating = at least 1.5 times as much and well outside the normal swing; Easing = two thirds or less; Quiet = too few articles to read; Steady = in between. News can rise without more fighting, so check the events too.
Preliminary UCDP records of organised violence with at least one death, each with a place and a date, released monthly and revised later.
How fast consumer prices rise over a year. High inflation erodes wages, savings and fixed-price contracts.

link.label: Inflation: Prices on the Rise (Back to Basics)

terms.definition: How much the economy grows in a year after removing inflation; negative = a shrinking economy.

link.label: Gross Domestic Product: An Economy's All (Back to Basics)

terms.definition: General government gross debt as a share of GDP. High debt leaves little room to respond to shocks.
Government revenue minus spending, as a share of GDP; negative = a budget deficit.
Trade, income and transfers with the rest of the world; a large deficit means relying on foreign money.
The central bank's foreign currency, expressed as how many months of imports it could pay for. Under 3 months is a common warning line.
The share of the labour force (or of 15–24-year-olds) who want work but have none.
The IMF's forecast for coming years in the World Economic Outlook; shown as dashed lines.
Prices rising fast while the economy stagnates or shrinks.
A sharp, often sudden fall in the value of a currency.
Government limits on moving money in or out of a country.
A loan from the IMF tied to policy conditions such as budget cuts or reforms.

categories.name: Governance (WGI)
categories.blurb: The six World Bank governance dimensions and how to read them.

terms.definition: Citizens' ability to choose their government; freedom of expression, association and the media.
Perceived likelihood of political instability and politically motivated violence, including terrorism.
Quality of public services, the civil service and policy delivery.
Ability to make and apply sound policies that let the private sector develop.
Confidence in contracts, property rights, the police and the courts.
How far public power is used for private gain, including state capture.
World Bank governance scores on a 0–100 scale (2025 methodology); higher = better governance.
The range the true WGI score lies in with 90% probability. If two years' ranges overlap, the change may be noise.
A change in a WGI score larger than its margin of error (the intervals don't overlap).

World Development Indicators (World Bank).

The UN Refugee Agency: displacement and refugee statistics.
Uppsala Conflict Data Program, the academic standard for armed-conflict data.
Global Database of Events, Language and Tone: global news monitoring, used as a backup news source and for media tone.
Calendar of national elections and referendums; the source of the event calendar dates.
UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.

terms.definition: Three-letter country codes, e.g. NGA for Nigeria.
Gross domestic product: the value of everything an economy produces in a year.

terms.definition: Public-domain map data; the source of the country outlines on the globe.
A saved copy of all the data (refreshed every week) so pages open instantly and keep working if a source is down.
Figures downloaded straight from the sources when the snapshot is over 10 days old, or with Refresh data; kept for 12 hours.
Dim to bright = lower to higher risk. Countries in dim dark grey are outside your filters; lighter grey means not enough data.
Stability = blue, Governance = orange, Economy = green, Social = amber, on maps, bars and tables.
Blue = safer than last year, grey = little change, red = riskier; brighter and taller = a bigger move.
On the globe, countries are raised by their score: the taller, the riskier.
Rings mark active armed conflict; the wider the ring, the more battle deaths.
Animated arcs run from refugees' country of origin (dim end) to the host country (bright end); thicker = more people.
Replays the index on the globe year by year since 2015.
Turn auto-rotation on or off, return to the starting view, zoom in and out.
Ctrl + scroll (⌘ on a Mac), a trackpad pinch or the + − buttons; a plain scroll moves the page. On a touch screen, tap the globe first, and Done hands swiping back to the page.
In the risk matrix and growth-vs-inflation chart, bubbles are sized by population.
A figure the IMF projects; the country has not reported it yet.
A 90% confidence interval (governance charts) or the middle half of countries (IMF outlook).
